question: What is the relative charge of a proton?
Which subatomic particle has no charge?
Where are protons and neutrons found in an atom?
An atom has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. How many neutrons does it have?
What are isotopes?
options: Atoms of different elements with the same mass number
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of electrons
Atoms of different elements with the same number of protons
correct: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons

question: How are elements arranged in the modern periodic table?
options: In order of increasing atomic mass
In order of increasing atomic number
correct: In order of increasing atomic number

question: What do elements in the same group of the periodic table have in common?
options: The same number of electron shells
The same number of electrons in their outer shell
correct: The same number of electrons in their outer shell

question: Which group of the periodic table contains the alkali metals?
What is produced when potassium reacts with water?
Which halogen is the most reactive?
Why are noble gases unreactive?
options: They have a full outer shell of electrons
They are gases at room temperature
They have very low mass numbers
correct: They have a full outer shell of electrons

question: What did Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment prove?
options: The atom is a solid sphere
The atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus
correct: The atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus

question: Which model of the atom described electrons embedded in a sphere of positive charge?
An atom of sodium has the electronic configuration 2,8,1. How many electron shells does it have?
Chlorine water is added to a solution of potassium iodide. What would you observe?
options: No reaction — chlorine is less reactive than iodine
The solution turns brown as iodine is displaced
The solution turns green as chlorine dissolves
correct: The solution turns brown as iodine is displaced

question: The number of protons in an atom is called the __________ number.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus is called the __________ number.
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are called __________.
Elements in the same vertical column of the periodic table are in the same __________.
Elements in the same horizontal row of the periodic table are in the same __________.
Group 1 metals react with water to produce a metal hydroxide and __________ gas.
The reactivity of Group 1 metals __________ going down the group.
Halogens exist as __________ molecules, for example Cl₂ and Br₂.
The alpha scattering experiment led to the replacement of the plum pudding model with the __________ model.
A charged particle formed when an atom gains or loses electrons is called an __________.
Match each subatomic particle to its relative charge and mass.
Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.definition: A substance made of only one type of atom
Two or more elements chemically bonded together
Two or more substances not chemically combined
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons

question: Match each group to its correct description.

pairs.definition: Alkali metals — very reactive, one outer electron, react with water
Halogens — reactive non-metals, seven outer electrons, exist as diatomic molecules
Noble gases — full outer shell, very unreactive, monatomic
Hard, dense metals in the centre of the periodic table, form coloured compounds

question: Match each atomic model to its key feature.

pairs.definition: Electrons embedded in a sphere of positive charge
Small, dense, positively charged nucleus with electrons orbiting around it
Electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels (shells)

question: Match each halogen to its state at room temperature.
State what is meant by the atomic number of an element.
mark_scheme: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom (1).

question: State what is meant by the mass number of an atom.
mark_scheme: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus (1).

question: Define the term isotope.
mark_scheme: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons (1).

question: State the trend in reactivity going down Group 1.
mark_scheme: Reactivity increases going down Group 1 (1).

question: State the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in an atom of carbon-12 (atomic number 6).
mark_scheme: 6 protons (1); 6 neutrons (1); 6 electrons (1) — any two for 2 marks.

question: Explain why elements in the same group of the periodic table have similar chemical properties.
mark_scheme: Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell (1); the number of outer electrons determines how an element reacts chemically (1).

question: Describe what is observed when lithium is added to water.
mark_scheme: Lithium floats and moves around the surface (1); fizzing / bubbling as hydrogen gas is produced (1); lithium dissolves to form a colourless solution of lithium hydroxide (1) — any two.

question: Explain why the reactivity of Group 1 metals increases going down the group.
mark_scheme: Going down the group, the outer electron is in a higher energy shell / further from the nucleus (1); it is more easily lost / less attracted to the nucleus (1).

question: Explain why the reactivity of halogens decreases going down Group 7.
mark_scheme: Going down the group, the outer shell is further from the nucleus (1); electrons are gained less easily / the atom is less able to attract an additional electron (1).

question: Describe the plum pudding model of the atom.
mark_scheme: The atom was modelled as a sphere of positive charge (1); with electrons embedded throughout it like plums in a pudding (1).

question: Explain what the results of the alpha scattering experiment showed about the structure of the atom.
mark_scheme: Most alpha particles passed straight through — the atom is mostly empty space (1); some were deflected at large angles — there is a small, dense, positively charged nucleus (1).

question: State two properties of transition metals that differ from Group 1 metals.
mark_scheme: Any two from: higher melting points (1); harder / denser (1); less reactive (1); can form coloured compounds (1); can act as catalysts (1).

question: Explain what happens in a halogen displacement reaction. Use chlorine and potassium bromide as an example.
mark_scheme: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine (1); chlorine displaces bromine from potassium bromide solution (1); potassium chloride and bromine are formed / solution turns orange-brown (1).

question: Describe how electrons are arranged in the shells of an atom. State the maximum number of electrons in the first three shells.
mark_scheme: Electrons occupy shells / energy levels around the nucleus (1); first shell holds up to 2 electrons (1); second and third shells hold up to 8 electrons each (1).

question: Explain how Mendeleev's periodic table differed from earlier attempts and why his table was accepted by scientists.
mark_scheme: Mendeleev arranged elements in order of atomic mass (1); left gaps for undiscovered elements (1); predicted the properties of missing elements (1); when these elements were discovered with the predicted properties, his table was accepted (1) — any three.

question: Explain how our model of the atom has changed over time, from the plum pudding model to the Bohr model. Include the evidence that led to each change.
mark_scheme: Plum pudding model: electrons embedded in a positive sphere (1); alpha scattering experiment — most particles passed through / some deflected at large angles (1); led to nuclear model: small dense positive nucleus with electrons orbiting (1); Bohr proposed electrons orbit in fixed energy levels / shells based on further experimental evidence (1).

question: Describe the trends in properties of the Group 1 alkali metals as you go down the group. Include reactivity, melting point, and reactions with water.
mark_scheme: Reactivity increases down the group (1); melting point decreases down the group (1); all react with water to form metal hydroxide and hydrogen (1); reactions become more vigorous down the group e.g. lithium fizzes, sodium melts and moves, potassium ignites (1).

question: Explain what is meant by relative atomic mass and why it is not always a whole number. Use the concept of isotopes in your answer.
mark_scheme: Relative atomic mass is the weighted average mass of atoms of an element (1); compared to 1/12 the mass of carbon-12 (1); most elements have more than one isotope with different mass numbers (1); the Ar is calculated taking into account the relative abundance of each isotope (1).

question: Compare the properties and reactivity of Group 7 halogens. Include physical appearance, state at room temperature, and trend in reactivity.
mark_scheme: Halogens exist as diatomic molecules (1); going down the group: boiling point increases, colour darkens (1); fluorine — pale yellow gas, chlorine — green gas, bromine — orange-brown liquid, iodine — grey-black solid (1); reactivity decreases down the group as outer shell is further from nucleus (1).

question: Explain how the structure of an atom determines its position in the periodic table and its chemical properties. Refer to atomic number, electron configuration, and group number in your answer.
mark_scheme: Atomic number = number of protons, determines the element and its position in the table (1); elements arranged in order of increasing atomic number (1); number of electron shells determines the period (1); number of outer electrons determines the group (1); outer electrons determine chemical properties — elements in the same group react similarly (1).

question: Evaluate the similarities and differences between Group 1 metals and transition metals. In your answer, consider physical properties, reactivity, and uses.
mark_scheme: Group 1: soft, low density, low melting point, very reactive (1); transition metals: hard, dense, high melting point, much less reactive (1); both are metals and good conductors of heat and electricity (1); transition metals can form coloured compounds / act as catalysts — Group 1 cannot (1); Group 1 reacts vigorously with water / air; transition metals do not react readily with water (1); uses: transition metals used in construction / catalysts / jewellery due to strength and low reactivity; Group 1 used in specialist applications e.g. lithium batteries (1).

question: Evaluate how scientific models of the atom have developed over time. Explain why models change and what this tells us about the nature of science.
mark_scheme: Early model: solid indivisible sphere (Dalton) (1); plum pudding model — electrons in positive sphere (Thomson) (1); nuclear model from alpha scattering — small dense nucleus (Rutherford) (1); Bohr model — electrons in fixed shells based on new evidence (1); models change when new experimental evidence cannot be explained by the existing model (1); science is a process of developing and refining ideas — no model is permanent / models are the best explanation based on current evidence (1).

question: Explain how the relative atomic mass (Ar) of an element is calculated. Include the terms relative isotopic mass and percentage abundance.
mark_scheme: Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean mass of an atom of an element compared to 1/12 the mass of carbon-12 (1); calculated using: Ar = Σ(isotopic mass × % abundance) ÷ 100 (1); e.g. chlorine: (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100 = 35.5 (1); different isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons (1).

question: Describe the arrangement of electrons in the first three shells of an atom. Use phosphorus (atomic number 15) as an example.
mark_scheme: Electrons occupy shells/energy levels around the nucleus (1); first shell: max 2 electrons; second shell: max 8; third shell: max 8 (1); phosphorus has 15 electrons (1); electron configuration: 2, 8, 5 (1).

question: Explain how the periodic table is arranged and what determines an element's position.
mark_scheme: Elements arranged in order of increasing atomic (proton) number (1); arranged in periods (rows) — period number = number of electron shells (1); arranged in groups (columns) — group number = number of outer shell electrons (1); elements with similar properties in same group — same number of outer electrons (1).

question: Describe how the discovery of the electron and the results of the alpha particle scattering experiment changed the model of the atom.
mark_scheme: Thomson discovered the electron — proposed 'plum pudding model' (positive sphere with embedded electrons) (1); Rutherford fired alpha particles at gold foil — most passed through, some deflected, a few bounced back (1); this showed the atom is mostly empty space with a small, dense, positive nucleus (1); Bohr later refined the model — electrons in fixed orbits at set energy levels (1).

question: Explain why the elements in Group 1 (alkali metals) become more reactive down the group.
mark_scheme: Group 1 elements have 1 outer shell electron — they react by losing this electron (1); going down the group, the outer electron is in a higher energy shell — further from the nucleus (1); more shielding from inner shells — nuclear attraction is weaker (1); outer electron lost more easily — more reactive (1).

question: Describe the reactions of Group 7 elements (halogens) and explain the trend in reactivity down the group.
mark_scheme: Halogens react by gaining one electron to form negative ions (halide ions) (1); reactivity decreases down the group (1); going down: outer shell further from nucleus, more shielding (1); electron gained less easily — lower reactivity (1).

question: Explain why elements in the same group of the periodic table have similar chemical properties.
mark_scheme: Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in the outer shell (1); chemical reactions involve outer shell electrons (1); same number of outer electrons means similar reactions (1); e.g. Group 1 all react with water to form hydroxide and hydrogen gas (1).

question: Describe the structure of an atom. Include the location, mass and charge of protons, neutrons and electrons.
mark_scheme: Nucleus contains protons and neutrons (1); proton: mass 1, charge +1; neutron: mass 1, charge 0 (1); electrons surround nucleus in shells: mass ~0 (1/1840), charge −1 (1); atom is electrically neutral — equal numbers of protons and electrons (1).

question: Evaluate the displacement reaction between chlorine water and potassium bromide solution. Include observations and ionic equation.
mark_scheme: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine (1); chlorine displaces bromide ions from solution (1); Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂ — orange/brown colour appears as bromine formed (1); ionic equation: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂ — shows oxidation of Br⁻ (1).

question: Explain the term 'isotope'. Use carbon-12 and carbon-14 as examples and explain why they have different masses.
mark_scheme: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons (1); carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons (1); carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons (1); different mass number because mass is mainly due to protons and neutrons (1).

question: Describe the properties of the noble gases (Group 0). Explain why they are unreactive.
mark_scheme: Noble gases are colourless gases at room temperature (1); very low boiling points — non-polar atoms with weak intermolecular forces (1); full outer electron shells — no tendency to gain or lose electrons (1); chemically inert / unreactive — used in light bulbs, neon signs, balloons (1).

question: Explain how our model of the atom developed from Dalton to the current nuclear model. Include the key scientists and their contributions.
mark_scheme: Dalton: atoms are indivisible spheres — first scientific atomic theory (1); Thomson: discovered electron — proposed plum pudding model (positive sphere, electrons embedded) (1); Rutherford: alpha scattering — discovered nucleus is small, dense and positive; most atom is empty space (1); Bohr: electrons in fixed orbits at fixed energy levels (1); modern quantum model: electrons in probability clouds/orbitals, not fixed paths (1).

question: Describe how mass spectrometry is used to identify elements and calculate relative atomic mass. Include how the instrument works and what the output shows.
mark_scheme: Sample is vaporised then ionised — atoms lose electrons, become positive ions (1); ions accelerated by electric field and deflected by magnetic field (1); amount of deflection depends on mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) (1); detector produces a spectrum — peaks at different m/z values show different isotopes (1); Ar calculated using peak heights (relative abundance) and m/z values of each isotope (1).

question: Explain how Mendeleev's periodic table differed from earlier attempts and why it was more successful as a model.
mark_scheme: Newlands: arranged by atomic mass, every 8th element similar — Law of Octaves (1); Mendeleev: also arranged by atomic mass but left gaps for undiscovered elements (1); predicted properties of missing elements — e.g. germanium (eka-silicon) (1); predictions confirmed when elements later discovered — validated the model (1); also swapped elements where atomic mass order didn't match properties — showed atomic number matters more than mass (1).

question: Evaluate the reactivity trend in Group 1 metals using the reactions with water as evidence. Include observations and balanced equations.
mark_scheme: All Group 1 metals react with water: metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen (1); Li: reacts steadily, floats and fizzes (1); Na: more vigorous, melts into a ball, faster fizzing (1); K: ignites — burns with lilac flame, very vigorous (1); Cs/Rb: explosively reactive — confirms increasing reactivity down group due to weaker nuclear pull on outer electron (1).

question: Explain the trends in physical properties (melting point, reactivity) of the halogens down Group 7. Include the states at room temperature for F, Cl, Br and I.
mark_scheme: Fluorine: pale yellow gas; chlorine: green gas; bromine: orange-brown liquid; iodine: grey solid (1); melting and boiling points increase down the group (1); stronger intermolecular forces as molecules get larger (1); reactivity decreases down the group — harder to gain an electron as outer shell is further from nucleus with more shielding (1); displacement reactions confirm trend: Cl₂ displaces Br⁻ and I⁻; Br₂ displaces only I⁻ (1).

question: Describe how flame tests and emission spectra provide evidence for electron energy levels. Include what causes the light and what results are seen for sodium and copper.
mark_scheme: Electrons absorb energy from flame — excited to higher energy levels (1); electrons fall back to ground state, emitting photons of light (1); wavelength of light corresponds to specific energy gap — unique to each element (1); sodium: bright yellow/orange flame (1); copper: green/blue-green flame — different energy gaps produce different colours (1).

question: Evaluate how the discovery of new elements in the 19th century tested and confirmed Mendeleev's periodic table.
mark_scheme: Mendeleev left gaps in his table and predicted properties of undiscovered elements (1); gallium (1875): properties matched Mendeleev's 'eka-aluminium' prediction closely (1); germanium (1886): closely matched 'eka-silicon' prediction for density, valency, oxide formula (1); this confirmatory evidence gave strong scientific credibility to periodic law (1); one exception: noble gases (Group 0) not predicted — but fitted without disrupting arrangement (1).

question: Describe the industrial uses of the halogens. Include uses of chlorine, fluorine and iodine.
mark_scheme: Chlorine: water purification — kills bacteria and pathogens (1); used in PVC/chlorinated polymers (1); fluorine: used in PTFE (non-stick coating) and toothpaste fluoride (strengthens enamel) (1); iodine: antiseptic (iodine solution); iodine-125 used in radiotherapy (1); bromine: used in flame retardants and some medicines (1).

question: Explain why the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus. Include the relative masses of subatomic particles and the scale of the atom.
mark_scheme: Protons and neutrons both have relative mass of 1 (1); electrons have relative mass of approximately 1/1840 — negligible (1); nucleus contains all protons and neutrons — most of the mass (1); nucleus is very small: ~1/10,000 of atomic radius (1); atom is mostly empty space — electrons occupy a volume much larger than the nucleus (1).

question: Evaluate the evidence that supports the reactivity trend in Group 7 (halogens). Include displacement reactions with halide salts and what these show about electron affinity.
mark_scheme: More reactive halogens displace less reactive ones from their salts (1); Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂ — chlorine displaces bromine (1); Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂ — chlorine displaces iodine (1); Br₂ + 2KI → 2KBr + I₂ — bromine displaces iodine (1); iodine cannot displace chlorine or bromine — confirms I is least reactive; trend explained by decreasing nuclear attraction for incoming electron down group (1).

question: Explain how the results of Rutherford's gold foil experiment led to the nuclear model of the atom. Include what was expected, what was observed, and what conclusions were drawn.
mark_scheme: Previous model: Thomson's plum pudding — positive spread throughout atom; expected most alpha particles to pass straight through (1); observed: most alpha particles did pass straight through (1); small number deflected at large angles (1); tiny fraction bounced directly back (1); conclusions: most atom is empty space (most pass through) (1); small, dense, positively charged nucleus exists (deflections caused by electrostatic repulsion from nucleus) (1).

question: Evaluate the development of the periodic table. Include Newlands, Mendeleev and modern understanding. Consider how the table was improved over time and the role of evidence.
mark_scheme: Newlands (1864): arranged by atomic mass, grouped every 8th element — noticed periodicity (1); limitation: failed for heavier elements; included metals and non-metals in same group — not accepted by scientific community (1); Mendeleev (1869): also ordered by mass but left gaps, switched some elements — predicted undiscovered elements (1); discoveries of gallium, germanium confirmed predictions — table accepted (1); modern: ordered by atomic number after Moseley's X-ray work — resolved anomalies (Ar before K) (1); noble gases added as Group 0 without disrupting arrangement — shows flexibility of the model (1).

question: Explain the concept of atomic number, mass number and isotopes. Calculate the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in ²⁷₁₃Al and ³⁷₁₇Cl⁻. Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties.
mark_scheme: Atomic number = number of protons (1); mass number = protons + neutrons (1); ²⁷₁₃Al: 13 protons, 14 neutrons, 13 electrons (neutral atom) (1); ³⁷₁₇Cl⁻: 17 protons, 20 neutrons, 18 electrons (gained 1 electron) (1); isotopes have same number of protons — same electron configuration (1); chemical properties determined by electron configuration — isotopes react identically (1).

question: Describe the reactions of the alkali metals (Group 1) with oxygen, water and chlorine. Include observations and why reactivity increases down the group.
mark_scheme: With oxygen: metal burns to form metal oxide — e.g. 4Li + O₂ → 2Li₂O; vigour increases down group (1); with water: metal + water → hydroxide + hydrogen — 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂; K ignites the hydrogen (1); with chlorine: metal + chlorine → metal chloride — 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl; more vigorous down group (1); reactivity increases: outer electron in higher shell (1); greater shielding reduces nuclear attraction on outer electron (1); outer electron lost more easily — lower ionisation energy (1).

question: Evaluate the properties and uses of the halogens. Consider their reactivity, states at room temperature, industrial importance and associated hazards.
mark_scheme: Fluorine: most reactive halogen; colourless/pale yellow gas; used in PTFE coatings; extremely toxic and corrosive (1); chlorine: green gas, less reactive; used for water purification and PVC; toxic — chlorine gas was used as a chemical weapon (1); bromine: orange-brown liquid; used in flame retardants; causes skin burns (1); iodine: grey solid; antiseptic; essential trace element for thyroid hormone (1); all decrease in reactivity down group — explained by increasing atomic radius and shielding (1); uses reflect their reactivity: less reactive halogens (iodine) safe for medical use; fluorine too reactive for most uses (1).

question: Explain what is meant by the term 'periodicity'. Include examples of trends in atomic radius, ionisation energy and electronegativity across Period 2.
mark_scheme: Periodicity: regular repeating patterns in properties of elements across each period (1); atomic radius: decreases across a period — more protons, stronger nuclear pull on same shell electrons (1); ionisation energy: generally increases across a period — same shielding, more protons (1); electronegativity: increases across a period — more protons attract bonding electrons more strongly (1); from Li to Ne: Li metallic and highly reactive; O and F non-metallic and electronegative; Ne unreactive (1); trends repeat in each period — explains the periodicity of the table (1).

question: Describe the chemistry of Group 0 (noble gases). Explain why they are chemically inert and discuss their industrial and scientific uses.
mark_scheme: Noble gases: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon (1); full outer electron shells — no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons (1); chemically inert under normal conditions (1); helium: used in balloons and airships — less dense than air, non-flammable unlike hydrogen (1); neon: used in fluorescent lights and neon signs — glows red-orange when electricity passed through (1); argon: used in light bulbs and welding — prevents oxidation of filament/metal; used in double-glazing for insulation (1).

question: Explain how ionisation energies provide evidence for electron shells and sub-shells. Include what ionisation energy is and the trend you would see when successive ionisation energies of sodium are plotted.
mark_scheme: First ionisation energy: energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms (1); successive ionisation energies increase as each electron removed from increasingly positive ion (1); Na has electron configuration 2,8,1; first IE very low — outer electron easily removed (1); large jump after 1st IE — 2nd electron from inner shell (1); another large jump after 9th IE — 10th electron from innermost shell (1); pattern of jumps provides direct evidence for separate electron shells (1).

question: Describe the trend in reactivity of Group 2 (alkaline earth metals) and explain this using atomic structure. Compare with Group 1.
mark_scheme: Group 2 metals have 2 outer shell electrons — lose both to form 2+ ions (1); reactivity increases down the group (1); increasing atomic radius and shielding — outer electrons lost more easily (1); less reactive than Group 1 — must lose 2 electrons vs 1 (higher ionisation energy) (1); e.g. Mg reacts slowly with water; Ca reacts vigorously; Ba reacts very vigorously (1).
